paras: The threat against Dave Leecraft was a written death threat sent in October 1888 to a Black porter in Charlotte, North Carolina, after he publicly announced that he would vote for Cleveland. The letter, decorated with drawn coffins and signed "The Republican Executive Committee," warned that he would not live to see November 6 unless he renounced the Democratic party. No violence against him was reported, but the dispatch ran in papers from Pennsylvania to Nebraska as an example of "Ku-Klux" intimidation of a Black Democrat.

Leecraft was described as a "well known negro porter for a leading hardware store" in Charlotte. On Tuesday morning he published a card in the Chronicle saying he would vote for Cleveland and advising his "colored friends" to do the same. The local Charlotte Democrat welcomed the card with the words "They are coming" and remarked that he argued the tariff question "very intelligently." According to the wire account, the card "created a sensation among the negroes," who heard of it from their leaders, and it was discussed for two days on street corners.

On Wednesday Leecraft received a letter "written in ignorant chirography" on the back of a Republican circular, with rudely drawn coffins bearing the words "Liberty or death." Described as being in "old time Ku-Klux style," it contained "the usual death resolutions" and threatened that he would not live to see November 6 unless he wrote another card renouncing the Democratic party.
The coverage contains no report of an investigation, of anyone being identified as the writer, or of any later attack on Leecraft.

The dispatch spread through the white press, appearing in the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer on October 25, the St. Paul Daily Globe on October 26, the Beatrice Daily Express on October 29 and the Butler Weekly Times on October 31. Headlines blamed the Republicans, among them "A Ku-Klux Notice Sent to a Colored Man," "Republican Ku-Klux" and "North Carolina Kuklux Threaten Death Under the Name of the Republican Executive Committee." The Lancaster paper ran the story among items on Black voters and Republicans turning to the Democrats.

In North Carolina the Edenton Fisherman & Farmer reprinted the wire on November 2 as "A Democratic Negro Threatened." The Asheville Citizen gave its own version, saying the threatening letters came "from his own color," and paired it with a Goldsboro Black editor's reported call for lashes for Black Democratic voters. From these it asked whether "the white man" could be "justified in voting with a party so largely made up of negroes."

The wire dispatch identified the sender only by the letter's signature and its Republican circular, while the Asheville Citizen alone attributed the letters to Black writers and spoke of more than one letter. Most copies put the letter on the Wednesday after the card, though the St. Paul Daily Globe's version, datelined October 25, said it arrived that day.

reader.title: Threat against Dave Leecraft
bases: The only act reported is an anonymous written death threat, decorated with drawn coffins, sent to a Black man over his public support for Cleveland; no violence followed in any report (A1, A2, A5).
No one was killed: Leecraft received a threatening letter, purportedly from a party committee, warning he would not live to see November 6 (A1, A2, A7). The coverage reports no attack on him.

Every detailed account is one Charlotte wire dispatch reprinted (A1, A2, A4, A6, A7); the Asheville Citizen's brief paragraph agrees a coffin-marked threat was sent but is of unclear independence and differs on who sent it (A5), and the local Charlotte Democrat mentions only the card (A3).

accounts.label: Charlotte Democrat (local)
accounts.gist: Notes only that Leecraft wrote a card announcing he would vote for Cleveland and argued the tariff 'very intelligently'.

framing.detail: Northern and Western papers reprinted the dispatch under headlines such as 'A Ku-Klux Notice Sent to a Colored Man', 'Republican Ku-Klux' and 'Coffin Embellisments', the Lancaster Intelligencer setting it among items on 'Colored Democrats'.
The Asheville Citizen, a Democratic paper, attributed the letters to Black writers and used them to ask whether white men could be 'justified in voting with a party so largely made up of negroes'.
The Edenton Fisherman & Farmer ran the wire under 'A Democratic Negro Threatened'; the local Charlotte Democrat greeted the card with 'They are coming' and did not mention a threat.
